cultural.vision_reason: The ostracon shows a painted drawing of Ramesses II being suckled by a goddess, an ancient Egyptian New Kingdom artifact clearly matching the claimed Egyptian ethnicity; it is a painted drawing on stone rather than a carved sculpture.

physical.title: Ostracon: Ramesses II Suckled by a Goddess
physical.summary: Ostraca (singular, ostracon) are natural limestone flakes, common to the region of Thebes. The ancient Egyptians who lived there, particularly the artisans of the royal tombs, used them extensively as writing or drawing surfaces, both for practice and for instruction. Some are almost finished works of art; others are clearly sketches. Whether passing idle time or practicing their technique, these pieces provide a rare look at an ancient artist at work. This ostracon is decorated with a scene of the king suckled by a goddess. Although his body is that of an adult, the king (identified by the inscriptions as Ramesses II) appears child size. The goddess wears a long garment of vulture's wings--she could be any of a number of protective mother or sky goddesses.

location.made_in_place: Egypt, New Kingdom (1540–1069 BCE), Dynasty 19, reign of Ramesses II (1279–1213 BCE)
